title: Polygon Angle Sums
trouble: Students think the exterior angles add to more for polygons with more sides, when the sum is always 360°.

blocks.html: You proved in Triangle Sum and Exterior Angle Proofs that a triangle's angles add to $180^\circ$. Every polygon can be cut into triangles, so the same fact gives the angle sum of any polygon.

Interior angles. In a convex polygon with $n$ sides, draw every diagonal from one vertex. They cut it into $n - 2$ triangles (each side except the two at that vertex gets its own triangle), and the triangles' angles together make up exactly the polygon's angles. So the sum is $(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$.
Exterior angles. At each vertex, the interior and exterior angles form a linear pair, so all $n$ pairs total $n \cdot 180^\circ$. Subtract the interior sum: $n \cdot 180^\circ - (n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ = 360^\circ$. It is one full turn, the amount you turn while walking once around the polygon.

blocks.cap: The diagonals from $A$ cut the pentagon into 3 triangles. Drag the corners (keep it convex): the five angles in the readout always add to $3 \cdot 180^\circ = 540^\circ$.

blocks.html: The interior angles of a convex $n$-gon add to $(n - 2) \cdot 180^\circ$. The exterior angles, one at each vertex, always add to $360^\circ$.

blocks.title: A missing angle
blocks.q: A hexagon has angles $110^\circ$, $135^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $140^\circ$, $95^\circ$ and $x^\circ$. Find $x$.

blocks.html: Thinking the exterior angles add to more when there are more sides. The interior sum grows by $180^\circ$ with each new side, but the exterior sum stays $360^\circ$: more exterior angles, each one smaller. Check: a square has four $90^\circ$ exterior angles and a regular octagon has eight $45^\circ$ ones; both total $360^\circ$.
